title: Install and maintain borehole and wellpoint pump systems

lessons.title: Groundwater basics and hazards
lessons.html:
Hydrology for boreholes and wellpoints

Groundwater is water stored in the spaces and cracks of soil and rock below the water table. A layer that holds and yields useful water is an aquifer.

  • Wellpoints are used in shallow, sandy aquifers, such as coastal sands in the Cape Flats or along the KZN coast. A perforated pipe with a screen is driven or jetted into the sand a few metres below the water table, and a surface pump sucks water up.
  • Boreholes are drilled into deeper aquifers, often in fractured rock. A pump is installed down the hole because water must be lifted further than a surface pump can suck.

Key terms

TermMeaning
Rest (static) water levelWater level when not pumping
Pumping (dynamic) water levelLower level while pumping
DrawdownDifference between rest and pumping levels
YieldFlow a source can supply sustainably
Suction liftHeight a surface pump must suck; limited in practice to about 7 m at sea level and less at altitude

Over-pumping lowers water levels, draws in sand and, near the coast, can draw in salt water. Groundwater use may need to be registered or licensed under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

Hazards and precautions

  • Electricity: submersible pumps run on mains power, often three-phase. Only qualified electricians connect and test panels; isolate and lock out before work.
  • Lifting: pipe columns with a pump can weigh hundreds of kilograms; use a tripod with a rated winch or a crane truck, never lift by hand beyond safe limits.
  • Falling objects: keep the borehole capped; tools dropped down a hole are very costly to recover.
  • Open holes: uncapped boreholes and wellpoint pits are a danger to children and animals.
  • Pressure: release pressure before opening fittings.
  • Water contamination: seal the borehole head so surface water, fuel and manure cannot enter.

Wear safety boots, gloves and a hard hat when lifting equipment, as required under the OHS Act 85 of 1993.

lessons.title: Wellpoint and submersible borehole pump installation
lessons.html:
Constructing a wellpoint

  1. Choose a site away from septic tanks, kraals and fuel stores.
  2. Jet or drive the wellpoint (screen and riser pipe) into the sand to below the lowest expected water level.
  3. Flush the wellpoint until the water runs clear of sand.
  4. Connect the riser to the suction pipe of a self-priming centrifugal pump, with a foot valve or non-return valve to hold prime, and a vacuum-tight joint. Air leaks on the suction side stop the pump drawing.
  5. Keep suction pipe as short and straight as possible, rising steadily to the pump with no high points that trap air.
  6. Fit a gate valve, non-return valve and pressure gauge on the delivery side.
  7. Mount the pump on a firm base and protect it from weather and theft.

Installing a submersible centrifugal pump with HDPE pipe

  1. Confirm borehole depth, casing diameter, rest and pumping water levels and yield from the borehole test report.
  2. Select pump and motor to suit yield and required head; set the installation depth below the pumping water level but well above the bottom so it does not draw silt.
  3. Join the HDPE riser to the pump with the correct compression or threaded adaptor.
  4. Tape the drop cable to the pipe every few metres. Attach a stainless steel safety rope to the pump and to the borehole cap to hold the pump if the pipe fails.
  5. Install level electrodes or a dry-run protection device so the pump switches off if the water drops.
  6. Lower the assembly slowly with a tripod and winch, keeping cable unkinked.
  7. Fit the borehole cap with a sealed cable entry, and a non-return valve, gauge and valve on the surface.
  8. Have the electrician connect the control panel with overload protection.

Commissioning

Run the pump, check for clear water, measure flow and pressure, check motor current against the nameplate (electrician), and confirm protection devices trip correctly.

lessons.title: Progressive cavity pumps, maintenance and documentation
lessons.html:
Installing a progressive cavity pump with galvanised pipe

A progressive cavity (helical rotor) pump uses a steel rotor turning inside a rubber stator to push water up. It is driven from the surface by a motor, engine, wind or solar head through a drive shaft inside the rising main. It handles low yields and high heads well and is common on farms for stock watering.

  1. Assemble the pump element at the bottom of the first length of galvanised steel pipe.
  2. Join pipe lengths with sockets, using thread compound and pipe wrenches; tighten correctly so joints do not leak or unscrew.
  3. Insert drive shaft sections with their couplings and bearing spiders inside the pipe as each length goes down.
  4. Use pipe clamps on the borehole head between lifts so the column never hangs only from the winch.
  5. Set the depth below pumping water level, fit the discharge head and drive unit, and adjust shaft length as the manufacturer specifies.

Never run a progressive cavity pump dry; the rubber stator is destroyed within a short time without water to lubricate it.

Servicing and maintenance

CheckSign of a problem
Flow and pressure against commissioning valuesDrop shows wear, blockage or falling water level
Motor current and insulation (electrician)High current or low insulation resistance
Water qualitySand, colour or smell changes
Surface fittingsLeaks, faulty non-return valve, gauge damage
WellpointsLoss of prime, air leaks, screens clogging
Drive headsBelt wear, bearing noise, oil level

Pull the pump for inspection when performance drops: check impellers or stator, cable joints, pipe threads and safety rope. Replace worn parts with matching specifications.

Documentation

  • Installation record: date, location (GPS), borehole depth, water levels, pump and motor model and serial numbers, installation depth, pipe type and length, cable size
  • Commissioning test results
  • Service history and parts replaced
  • Water use records where required

Key points

  • Wellpoints suit shallow sand; boreholes need submersible or shaft-driven pumps.
  • Install pumps below the pumping water level with dry-run protection and a safety rope.
  • Only qualified electricians work on power supply and panels.
  • Never run a progressive cavity pump dry.
  • Keep full installation, test and service records.
